Hi Alex — thanks for the details. High-level guidance and an outline of a migration approach below. I kept the notes actionable so your infra team can evaluate quickly.

1) Dimension choice (768 vs 1536):
- 1536-d generally improves recall for large product catalogs, especially when using transformer-based encoders, but increases index size (~2x) and per-query compute.
- If your reranker is strong, staying at 768 and improving quantization + ANN config can be cheaper and close in quality. We recommend an A/B evaluation: sample ~100k queries, generate 1536 and 768 embeddings for a subset of your catalogue, and compare recall@K plus reranker delta.

2) Normalization & similarity:
- Use L2 normalization if you plan to use dot-product as proxy for cosine similarity in the ANN layer; L2 norm makes results comparable across dims.
- If your reranker expects cosine rankings, keep the pipeline consistent: compute cosine on the embedded vectors (either via normalized vectors or by using cosine-aware ANN).

3) Batching & SDK/runtime settings:
- For inference per-request: prefer batching at the SDK layer. Given your traffic, we suggest target batch sizes of 32–64 for CPU-bound endpoints and 16–32 for GPU-backed real-time endpoints (to keep 95p latency within 150ms).
- Enable async streaming for reranker pipeline to decouple retrieval from reranking where possible.
- SDK auth: Redwood SDK supports API keys and mTLS for private deployments. Example (pseudo):

  // JS SDK example (pseudo)
  import Redwood from '@redwood-ai/sdk'
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, endpoint: 'https://dedicated-us.redwood.ai' })
  const resp = await client.embeddings.create({ model: 'redwood-embedding-1536', input: textBatch, normalize: true })

- Routing: configure route policy to prefer dedicated pool (lower latency) and fallback to hosted burst pool; we can pre-configure a routing policy for your account.

4) Migration (zero / low-downtime approach):
- Phase 0 (prep): snapshot current index and export sample vectors (we’ll use your spreadsheet).
- Phase 1 (pilot): onboard a 10–20% shard to Redwood — produce 1536-d for that shard and run side-by-side evaluation (A/B) against the 768 index.
- Phase 2 (hybrid serving): serve both indexes in parallel for a short period. Use a routing rule to prefer Redwood for a growing % of traffic. Translate top-K from both stores into a merged candidate list (dedupe by ID) before reranking. This avoids immediate re-ranking regressions.
- Phase 3 (cutover): once metrics (recall, NDCG, latency) meet thresholds, re-index remaining shards; perform a final switch to Redwood-only routing.

5) Reranker considerations:
- Keep reranker input consistent (if you change dim or normalization, re-benchmark reranker quality).
- Optionally, run a mini-training loop on reranker using new embeddings to recover any distribution shift.

6) Quantization & cost:
- We support 8-bit and 4-bit quantized indexes; 8-bit is a good balance for recall vs storage. Quantization requires re-encoding the embeddings during indexing — plan for a reprocessing job.

7) Sample artifacts attached: migration template + minimal schema (see attachments). I also dropped a short SDK snippet and an internal eval checklist to the Drive link Marissa shared.

If you’re comfortable, here’s a proposed timeline for our teams:
- Tue 2026-04-07: pilot shard onboarding and perf test (1 week)
- Tue 2026-04-14: hybrid serving evaluation
- Early May: full re-index + cutover (depends on wheelhouse)

Let me know if you want us to produce the A/B perf matrix vs cost for 768/1536 + quantization — we can have that in 3 business days.
